analysis:
Examined the docs change in docs/provider/troubleshooting.md and the one-line code change in ProviderLoop+AddonHold.swift.

The docs change adds a troubleshooting row for lifecycle drain failures (head line 135) and documents the bounded-drain behavior. It is documentation only. It recommends `--force` only for providers without the bounded drain, and says force interrupts only unfinished work. I found no security-relevant claim that overstates a control, and no change to the receipt, attestation or authorization language. The remaining prose changes at head lines 169-171 (model recovery rows) describe memory-recovery behavior, not trust boundaries.

The code change is in `enterAddonHold()` (head lines 204-207). It now also cancels `selectedModelRecovery.attempt?.task` when an add-on hold begins. This tightens the TB-012 model-load fence and the T-059 intent that no model loads beside running VMs. It does not weaken the hold or open a new trust boundary. It does not affect the peer authentication in `handleAddonIPC`, `ownedHold`, lease enforcement or the machine-lock fallback.

Open integration questions, none of them a finding:
(1) The cancellation covers only the in-flight recovery attempt. Whether a later scheduled recovery tick or retry loop re-checks `addonHoldLoadRefusal` is not visible here, because the `selectedModelRecovery` implementation is outside the supplied evidence. The base fence `addonHoldLoadRefusal` (lines 340-343) should still refuse loads while a hold is active, but the recovery load path was not verified to call it.
(2) Whether cancelling the task sets state, such as a backoff or `Last check` text, correctly after release is also not verified.

T-059 and A-018 are the relevant threats and assets. I recommend a quick check that selected-model recovery honours the hold fence, but I found no evidence of a regression.
